topic: The Pi-Collision Mystery: From Bouncing Blocks to Digits of π

outline.topic: The Pi-Collision Mystery: From Bouncing Blocks to Digits of π

sections.title: The Setup: The Elastic Collision Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the physics of two blocks on a frictionless surface. Block A (mass m) moves towards Block B (mass M=100^n * m) which is initially at rest, with a wall behind B. Explain the conservation of momentum and kinetic energy.
sections.example: A small hamster-sized block (m) slides toward a giant elephant-sized block (M) sitting in front of a solid stone wall.

sections.title: The Pattern: Counting the Collisions
sections.content: Define the rule: Block A bounces off B, and B bounces off the wall. Observe the total collision count. For M=100m, total collisions = 31. For M=10,000m, total collisions = 314.
sections.example: Visual animation showing the small block ping-ponging between the wall and the large block, with a counter ticker in the corner of the screen incrementing rapidly.

sections.title: The Bridge: Geometry in Motion
sections.content: Explain the prerequisite: The motion of the two blocks can be mapped to a billiard ball bouncing inside a circular wedge. The angle of the wedge is determined by the mass ratio. The number of collisions represents the discrete approximation of the arc length.
sections.example: A split-screen graphic: Left side shows the blocks hitting; right side shows a dot moving along the circumference of a circle, hitting the x-axis, representing the 'collision' angles.

sections.title: The Revelation: Calculating Pi
sections.content: Connect the mass ratio to the digits of π. As the mass ratio increases by factors of 100, the collision count maps to the digits 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9... This illustrates how physical systems can serve as mechanical computers for irrational numbers.
sections.example: An animation of the digits of π (3.14159...) appearing on the screen as the mass of the large block increases exponentially.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Abstraction
sections.content: Summarize that what looks like a simple mechanical collision is actually a visual representation of a complex mathematical constant. Encourage students to view physical limits as windows into number theory.
sections.example: A final shot showing the blocks settling into a rhythmic motion that perfectly traces the curvature of π.
